content.title: Tuesday Morning Briefing
content.lead: The most important news to start your day: Tariff negotiations with Trump's administration after Canada's bold move; Europe's support for Ukraine; Embolo transfers to the U.S.

content.text: You can only read this in the NZZ: In the 1970s, Daniel Rossellat began organizing concerts in Nyon. This led to the Paléo Festival, which became Switzerland's largest festival with 250,000 attendees annually. Rossellat also shaped his hometown as city president. After 18 years, he left politics. Nevertheless, Rossellat continued to bubble with ideas; thanks to him, Switzerland would soon have its first Cultural Capital. Read the interview

content.title: The Most Important News This Morning
Canada breaks off tariff negotiations with the US – would that be an option for Switzerland too?

image.author: Carlos Osorio / Reuters
image.altText: A drone view shows a vehicle crossing the $4.7 billion Gordie Howe International Bridge, connecting Windsor, Ontario and Detroit, Michigan, the day after it opened in Windsor, Ontario, Canada, July 28, 2026. REUTERS/Carlos Osorio

content.text: What happened: Canada was the first country in a long time to leave the negotiating table with the U.S. and suspended ongoing negotiations for a tariff agreement. After Prime Minister Mark Carney announced this over the weekend, U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Monday that he would increase punitive tariffs on cars, car parts, and steel from Canada. Read the report

Why it matters: Canada’s approach was remarkable. Most governments had so far tried to remain in talks with the Trump administration to reach a trade agreement. Carney also surprised with his choice of words, stating that they were then «at war» because Canada had been attacked.

The question for Switzerland: Should Switzerland also have broken off tariff negotiations with the U.S.? At the time, no one in Switzerland was advocating for an end to the talks. However, there were certainly ideas for a tougher negotiating stance. These included selling U.S. stocks held by the National Bank, restricting gold trade with the U.S., or stopping deliveries of critical components.

Canada preferred to suffer rather than surrender: Prime Minister Carney remained true to his trade policy: no agreement with Washington was better than a bad one. Europe was advised to follow Canada's example. Read the «NZZ Pro» commentary

Tariffs were ruining business for Swiss machinery manufacturers: Losses for Swiss companies in the MEM sector in 2025 due to U.S. tariffs amounted to 1 billion Swiss francs. Business was still declining. Read the report

content.title: On Ukraine's Independence Day, London reaffirms support

content.text: What happened: Ukraine celebrated the 35th anniversary of its independence yesterday. In his speech, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy emphasized his country's will to resist: «Ukraine wants peace, but is not ready to simply surrender.» He called on partners for more support, especially for air defense. The most important pledge of the day concerned offensive weapons. Britain gave the green light for the transfer of important defense technology. Read the report

Why it matters: Russia sharply condemned that the Storm Shadow/Scalp cruise missile, based on British and French technology, could soon be produced in Ukraine. The guided missile had a range of 250 kilometers. «Britain is part of the war and regularly pours oil on the fire,» a Kremlin spokesman said.

The background: After the official celebrations, the so-called Coalition of the Willing held a hybrid meeting. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who made his first foreign trip since taking office in Kyiv, chaired the meeting. French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and many others participated via video. The U.S. was not represented. Read the live ticker
This was what the celebrations in the heart of Kyiv looked like: Watch the video

In the economic war against Iran, the U.S. government suddenly relied on «silent diplomacy»: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent refrained from imposing sanctions on Iran's trading partners at that time. He wanted to give the affected states one last chance — after previously threatening to bring Tehran to its knees. Read the report

Zurich's FDP lost its last district school presidency: The party narrowly lost to the SP in the election for the presidency of the Glattal district school board. The SP then led six of seven district school boards. After the election, the FDP criticized the GLP. Përparim Avdili, president of the Zurich City FDP, said: «My incomprehension could hardly be greater.» Read the report

Zurich voted on high-rise guidelines: On Sept. 27, voters would decide whether buildings up to 40 meters high could be constructed in the city. The City Council wanted to prevent this from being approved in large parts of Altstetten, Albisrieden, Wiedikon, Affoltern, Oerlikon, and Schwamendingen. Read the report

Swiss national striker Breel Embolo transferred to Atlanta: After only one year, the 29-year-old footballer broke off his long-term project at Stade Rennes. This caused irritation. However, the transfer from Ligue 1 to Major League Soccer's Atlanta United FC had a volume of over 15 million euros. Read the report

image.author: Photo: Chan Long Hei/AP
image.altText: FILE - Leticia Wong, former pro-democracy district councilor, arranges books at her bookstore in Hong Kong on June 20, 2025. (AP Photo/Chan Long Hei, File)

content.text: Bookselling as a crime: Leticia Wong and her partner sold books in Hong Kong. Then they went to prison. The accusation was that they had carried «seditious works.» In the past 12 months, Hong Kong law enforcement authorities had arrested at least 11 booksellers. The psychological profile of a city then on the verge of losing its soul: Read the «NZZ Pro» reportage

Poetic adventure: The Count of Velhoco, a district on the Canary Island of La Palma, hated official letters and bills. One day, when he had had enough, he wrote on his mailbox: «Solo cartas de amor» (only love letters). Indeed, people began to drop only love letters into it. The Count died three years ago. Since his death, his daughter had continued this unusual legacy. Read the background

Europe's dangerous missile gap: The West lacked interceptor missiles and long-range weapons for the war in Ukraine. The war against Iran exacerbated the deficit. This was more than a gap in the arsenal: against an adversary like Russia, which possessed a large arsenal of ballistic missiles, Europe lacked precisely those conventional options that lay between merely intercepting an attack and a significantly higher level of escalation. Read the «NZZ Pro» background

Record profits with pitfalls: AI investments were causing a profit surge in the U.S. In Europe, the profits of energy companies were inflating the overall result. But for strong profit growth to continue for a while, many things had to align. Read the analysis

🎧 Listen: Ukraine handled a significant portion of its exports through the ports around Odesa. At the time, Russia was intensifying attacks on the region. Far from the front, a decisive battle was being fought there. It was about Ukraine's economic survival. Foreign correspondent Jonas Roth traveled to Odesa to get a picture. In «NZZ Akzent,» he described how the city was trying to defend itself against Russia. Listen to the podcast

📖 Read: «The Oyster» was a novel of brilliant reflections. Yael Inokai, the writer born in Basel and living in Berlin, began her work with sharply etched scenes. What followed was a crime novel unfolding under Berlin's gray winter sky and, at the same time, a highly literary enigma. Read the review

We wish you a good start to the day.
Ulrike Putz, Klaus Bardenhagen, and Lillybelle Eisele
The briefing is published on weekdays at 6 AM and 5 PM. On Saturdays, there is a weekend edition at 7 AM.
